title: A Sampling Controller for Any Motion Model: Many Random Futures, Weighted by How Good They Are, and Why the Model Has to Be the Vehicle's

questions.question: What does a sampling controller need to know about the vehicle?
options: Its mass and its motor constants
A linear model about the path
A function that says where one step of control takes it
Nothing: it learns the vehicle as it drives
questions.explanation: The controller rolls candidate control sequences forward with that function and scores where they go. Any model that can be stepped will do.

questions.question: How many samples did the car test use?
questions.explanation: Each control step makes 100 noisy copies of the nominal sequence, rolls each out over 2 seconds and weights them by cost.

questions.question: Planning with a unicycle for the car, tracking error against the car's own model:
questions.explanation: Hardly different, because it replans every 0.1 s. The wrong model was no worse at tracking, because every plan starts from where the car really is. Its 2 second prediction was 0.67 m out, which matters for anything that relies on the prediction.

questions.question: A controller given the grid made how many poses in blocked cells?
options: 1, at the corner of the block
questions.explanation: A blocked cell adds a large cost to any rollout that enters it, so the weighted average steers round. Given no grid, the controller made 15 such poses.

questions.question: What does lambda do?
options: Sets how many of the worse rollouts still count in the weighted average
Sets how much noise is added to each control
Sets how far along the path the end cost looks
Sets how often the controller runs
questions.explanation: The weight of a rollout falls off with how much worse it is than the best, on a scale of lambda. Small lambda follows the best few and large lambda averages many.

questions.question: What is the price of more samples?
options: More rollouts every step, on the vehicle's processor
A lower control rate, by design
questions.explanation: 0.152 m error at 8 samples against 0.077 m at 100. Samples times horizon rollouts are computed every 0.1 s. Going from 8 to 100 halved the error and multiplied that work by twelve.
